render.title: How mitochondria make ATP from food molecules
render.body:
When you eat food, your digestive system breaks down carbohydrates into glucose. Cells then convert that glucose into ATP — the molecule they use as a direct energy source — through a process called cellular respiration. Most of this ATP is made inside the mitochondrion.

The process has three main stages:

1. Glycolysis (in the cytoplasm): Glucose is split into two molecules of pyruvate. This yields a small amount of ATP (a net gain of 2 ATP) and two NADH electron carriers.

2. Krebs cycle (in the mitochondrial matrix): Pyruvate is converted into acetyl-CoA, which enters the Krebs cycle. Each turn of the cycle releases carbon dioxide and passes high-energy electrons to carrier molecules (NADH and FADH2). Each acetyl-CoA yields 3 NADH, 1 FADH2, and 1 GTP.

3. Oxidative phosphorylation (on the inner mitochondrial membrane): NADH and FADH2 donate their electrons to the electron transport chain — a series of protein complexes embedded in the inner membrane. As electrons move along the chain, protons (H+) are pumped from the matrix into the intermembrane space, building up a proton gradient. Protons then flow back through ATP synthase, and that flow drives the synthesis of ATP. Oxygen accepts the final electrons at Complex IV, forming water.

The inner membrane is tightly sealed, so protons can only re-enter the matrix through ATP synthase. This coupling of the proton gradient to ATP production is called chemiosmosis.

Overall, complete oxidation of one glucose molecule can yield approximately 30 to 32 ATP under typical cellular conditions.
render.summary: Food is broken down to glucose, which goes through glycolysis, the Krebs cycle, and the electron transport chain. Proton flow through ATP synthase on the inner mitochondrial membrane produces most of the cell's ATP, with oxygen as the final electron acceptor.
